utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope you're well today. We will now continue the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, before we start we have been able last night to find the web site of the Ministry of Defence of FRY concerning the Law on Defence which is at tab 63, P984 here, and we had the problem about the second paragraph. Now, the document is in Serbian, but out of -- from the web site it clearly shows that there are three paragraphs in this law and we can distribute this to the Judges, to Professor, and to our learned friends from the OTP so maybe Professor can comment, if it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems sensible to do this, Mr. Hannis, and perhaps give it an IC number and mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, I'll have an argument at some point in time before you consider admitting it into evidence about when that was published on the web site and when it got to be three paragraphs, if it was always that way or only since yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hopefully that investigation will be continued by Mr. Zecevic and should be clarified but relevant. But when we've got the Professor here, we should hear the evidence subject to its admissibility being determined in due course. So in a sense -- not just in a sense, it would be a wider reservation than simply marking the document for identification. We will reserve the question of the admissibility of the answers given to questions about this document until the matter is either resolved or in the course of our final deliberations. So have you copies of this for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have copies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC133, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say tab 69?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it's at tab -- Your Honour, tab 63, P984, Article 4, second, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could I have one copy for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think even I can see the point just from looking at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, just a brief comment by Professor will do I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's precisely as I assumed yesterday, which means in performing the duties described in paragraph 2 which consist of eight items,"The president of the republic shall issue orders, commands, and decisions," this is what I assumed the case was yesterday. It says here: "In performing all of the duties described in paragraph 2," and paragraph 2 has a total of eight items.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, Professor, paragraph 2 begins with the following words: "In his command of the army, the president of the republic shall ..." and then follow eight items?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "... and in performing all of these eight duties, the president shall issue orders, commands, and decisions."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which is paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, which is paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you wish me to pursue this matter any further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't. I'm satisfied with --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that explanation of the document. What Mr. Hannis has to say about it, we'll consider in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. The -- just for the record, the web site from which this was taken is on the upper -- upper part of the first page. Thank you. Yesterday Your Honours requested us to provide the constitutional decision to which Professor Markovic was referring to. Now, unfortunately we have been unable to find that particular decision because the registry -- the Official Gazette registry concerning the decisions of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia for 1991 has like seven pages. And out of the description we couldn't really decide which document was -- which constitutional decision was actually the one which Professor was referring to. And of course there was no time for us to read through all of them. So what I -- what we are suggesting is that we provide a copy of the registry which we have over here, register -- Official Gazette register for the 1991 concerning the decisions of the Constitutional Court so Professor might be able during the -- one of the breaks to reflect -- refresh his memory and give us the particular decision that we have to provide to the -- to the honourable Trial Chamber and to him as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's an excellent suggestion, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If usher could -- we have prepared the copies for our colleagues from the Prosecution and the registry and for Professor. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, this is the register of decisions. You will be able to take a look at it during one of the breaks, and then perhaps after that you could give us your comment concerning that, or rather, your suggestion as to which one of all of those decisions could be the one that we referred to yesterday. Professor, during Prosecution case a certain number of regulations was admitted into evidence, regulations adopted in the period prior to the 1992 constitution, to be more precise, between 1988 and 1992. In paragraph 85 of the indictment, the Prosecution claims that in early 1989 the government of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia commenced a process which was aimed at taking away or revoking the autonomy of Kosovo. I suppose that this pertains to the Government of Serbia, not SFRY. This must be some kind of a mistake. So to revoke the autonomy that Kosovo had pursuant to the 1974 constitution. So, Professor, could we look at tab 72, 1D125. This is a document which is known as the blue book. The date it was published is 11th of March, 1977. The Presidency of the SFRY set up a working group, a body, which assessed the constitutional and legal position of Serbia in relation --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have it -- it is probably me, the -- 5, row 8, the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Serbia, not of SFRY. It's page 5, line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, this is tab 72?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 72, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't have a page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's transcript page 5, 8 -- row 8, where it says "Presidency of FRY -- of SFRY," and it should read: "Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Serbia." It's page 5, row 8 of the transcript, that is what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Serbia established a working group which assessed the constitutional and legal position of the Socialist Republic of Serbia and autonomous provinces, Vojvodina and Kosovo, that were within its composition in accordance with the decisions, or rather, in accordance with the solutions adopted in the 1974 constitution. Professor, at the very beginning on page 1 of this document, which is also the first paragraph of translation, it says that the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Serbia at a session held on the 16th of January, 1975, put forward an initiative to assess the issues of the constitutional organisation of the republic, particularly focusing on the implementation of functions that are of interest to the republic as a whole. Professor, on the 16th of January, 1975, how much time had elapsed at that time since the 1974 constitution on that date.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, the 1974 constitution was adopted in April, that means that this was less than a year after the constitution entered into force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The reason for such an initiative of the Presidency was based on what, very briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was in a contradictory position of autonomous provinces which existed only within the composition of one out of six republics. So those were the autonomous provinces within the constitutional system of one of the units of the Federation. Autonomous provinces existed within Serbia and were represented in the Federation independently, outside of Serbia, as though provinces were also subjects of the Federation. In addition to that, the level of autonomy of a province was almost identical to the level of autonomy of a republic so that the Republic of Serbia, when it came to its rights and duties within the SFRY, could exercise its rights and duties only outside of the territory of autonomous provinces; that is to say, the territory of Serbia proper, excluding autonomous provinces. This is why an issue of equality was raised of the Republic of Serbia in relation to other republics of the Yugoslav Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This material is quite voluminous, and we extracted only certain relevant portions of that material here. I think this is a book numbering about a hundred or so pages, correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the so-called blue book which was not available to the public for quite a long time, because you can see on page 1 it says "strictly confidential," and in that book, if one looks from this point of view, a critical view of the constitution, both of Serbia and the Federation, it takes a critical view of this issue, to follow-up on your previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps you should elicit from the witness an explanation of exactly what the blue book is, then it might put it in -- or put what's being said in context for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you heard Judge Bonomy's question, didn't you. Can you please explain what in actual fact the blue book was.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a criticism of the constitutional position, a critical analysis of the constitutional position of the Republic of Serbia within the constitutional system after 1974. This critical analysis was conducted by a working group comprising two university professors of political sciences at the time, Professor Najdan Pasic and Professor Radislav Ratkovic. There were a number of state officials involved as well. Specifically, I remember Mr. Veljko Markovic and Mr. Milivoj Draskovic, the then-republican secretary for legislation. Within the framework of this critical analysis, a comprehensive view was provided over dozens of pages in a very documented way of Serbia's constitutional position. Certain conclusions were drawn based on this. One of those, as far as I remember - I'm not sure if it is, in fact, included in your presentation - is that Serbia's constitutional position within a federation, that due to its very nature is an expression of the rights of the Yugoslav peoples to self-determination, jeopardizes the right of the Serbian people to the their own self-determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Professor, that's sufficient for present purposes. Let's concentrate now on the questions that Mr. Zecevic has for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we have highlighted some of the conclusions here. I'm now looking at page 3 of the document that we have prepared. Specifically I'm talking about paragraph 3 of the relevant translation. In the blue book itself the page number is 89, the page numbers are in the upper right corner of the page. Specifically I'm talking about paragraph 2. It begins: "These unresolved contradictions ..." Could you please comment on the three or four contradictions being specifically referenced on this page and the next page, page 90.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically it reads here that the constitutional position of the Republic of Serbia resulted in the creation of three different and in congress legal systems within the Republic of Serbia growing further and further apart, drifting further and further apart. There was one legal system in one of the provinces and another in the other province and yet a third system in the Republic of Serbia itself, which was not itself as structured as an autonomous province. But this entire territory is within the Republic of Serbia, where we see three parallel legal systems being established. The next thing is tendencies towards territorial isolation -- self-isolation exclusivity, not positioned to free self-managed integration. The provinces enjoyed all the attributes of statehood. Their constitutional executive and judicial authorities. Therefore, they were self-sufficient entities. As a result, within the Republic of Serbia itself, you had two states within a state in manner of speaking. Serbia itself had the status of a state, yet within its own body it had other states that were the autonomous provinces, which resulted in a splintering of Serbia's economy and jeopardised Serbia's internal domestic market. The fact that the provinces had a state-like character led to substantial differences in their respective education systems, exclusivity in media operations, cultural, sporting, and other activities, those were exclusively within the territorial limits of the provinces. The very fact that the autonomous provinces were represented within the Federation as independent units, that is, independent from the Republic of Serbia, and not within Serbia's own representation, cast a shadow on the possibility -- on the ability of Serbia as a republic to express its own positions and interests in the same way that the remaining five republics were able to, the remaining five republics that were members of the Yugoslav Federation. These are the conclusions of this analysis. There is one missing, one which we find at the very end of the blue book. This was a multi-national federation which was an expression of the self-determination of all of Yugoslavia's people, but it was the self-determination of the Serbian people that was at stake here, the Serbian people as one of the constituent peoples of Yugoslavia as a federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, briefly, if you could, please, explain why they were set up. What was the reason that the autonomous provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo were set up within the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first reason is historical background, the next reason would be the ethnic context, and the third reason would be the peculiarity of these areas in terms of their economies, their peculiarity in relation to the Republic of Serbia as a whole. When the autonomous provinces were set up, and they were first established in 1945, they were created for these very reasons. From day one they were part of the Republic of Serbia, and out of all the republics of the former Yugoslav Federation, the Republic of Serbia was the only republic to have within its body, as it were, two autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you talked about the ethnic make-up. How important a factor was that? To what extent did that affect the creation of the autonomous provinces? I'm talking about the ethnic make-up of the autonomous provinces, of course.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both these autonomous provinces, there were ethnic minorities, and these were represented to a large degree the Albanian minority in the case of Kosovo and Metohija and the Hungarian minority in the autonomous province of Vojvodina, in addition to which there were other minorities. However, some people back where we come from have an erroneous view of what the autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija and is supposed to mean. It is not the Albanians in Kosovo's territory enjoying this autonomy, but rather the entire population of Kosovo and Metohija, which is a mixed bag in terms of its ethnic make-up, if I may put it that way. There is -- there are a number of different ethnic minorities in Kosovo, in addition to which the area is very peculiar in terms of its history. Therefore, the autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija is not something that only involves the Albanian ethnic minority, nor is this supposed to be a solution to their position within Kosovo and Metohija. It is the entirety of these peculiarities that I have now addressed that constitutes the reason for Kosovo and Metohija to enjoy autonomy within the Republic of Serbia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Everything you are now saying about Kosovo, needless to say, mutatis mutandis applies to Vojvodina, does it not, regardless of the ethnic make-up of Vojvodina's population, where the Serbian people constitute a majority, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But even there we see a number of ethnic minorities. What's more, there are more ethnic minorities in Vojvodina than in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to have a clarification for my purposes. Now, Yugoslavia had federal units and Serbia also had these autonomous provinces, which according to yourself were quite independent. Now, why couldn't Yugoslavia have these also as independent federal units, having the same status as the rest? Why then have it within Serbia? Could there be any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason is that back at the time when they were first established, they happened to be in the territory of the Republic of Serbia. Another reason is that the Yugoslav Federation, in its very nature, was an expression of the right of all of Yugoslav's peoples to self-determination, the Serbs, the Croats, the Slovenes, the Montenegrins, the Bosnians, the Macedonians. It wasn't possible for the Serbs to exercise their right to self-determination multiply, that is in Vojvodina or among the Albanians because the Albanians were not a Yugoslav people. This is the reason that the Yugoslav Federation comprised only the republics, or rather, only those federal units that were expressions of the right of all of Yugoslavia's peoples to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, all of these ethnicities, in fact, had their own original states, don't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called them nationalities at the time because the expression "minority" had a number of negative connotations. It goes without saying that they all had their home countries, their home states. The Albanian minority, for example, had Albania, a neighbouring state at the time, a neighbor state of the SFRY, and the same thing applies to the Hungarian ethnic minority. Again, there was a shared border between the then-Federation of the SFRY and Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Might I ask a question? Professor, I'd like to know what factors would determine whether a particular group within Serbia became a constituent people as opposed to a minority group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Purely ethnic factors were at work and were decisive. What was required was an ethnic group that belonged to the south Slavic group. These groups were joined together in a state federation. At first it was called the FNRY and then later it was called the SFRY, the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. It was this ethnic character that provided a bench-mark for the establishment of the Yugoslav Federation. This is unequivocally addressed in a 1943 decision adopted at the 2nd Session of the so-called AVNOJ, the Anti-Fascist League of Yugoslavia's National -- the Anti-Fascist Council of Yugoslavia's National Liberation. This was some sort of a provisional parliament that was established during the war of liberation against fascism. The decision was then taken that once the war was over Yugoslavia would be established in the form of a federation comprising on an equal footings all of the Yugoslav peoples, and then these groups are listed as I have listed them before. These would have republics, and these republics would constitute the federal units of the federation. The first constitution after the country's liberation, that is, after the Second World War, the constitution of the Federal National Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted in 1946. In terms of both norm and constitutional right, this decision was adopted at the 2nd Session of the AVNOJ, A-V-N-O-J. For as long as the Yugoslav Federation existed, this decision lay at the very foundation of the Federation. This is the founding idea, if you like, of the Yugoslav Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, to go back to the blue book. You have already explained to us what conclusions the working group reached, and if I understand it correctly, the only way for that situation which was established in 1977 over a three-year period, or rather, three years after the 1974 constitution was adopted, for that situation to be brought into line with the situation in the other members of the Federation, the only way to do that was to amend the Constitution of Serbia. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to amend the Constitution of Serbia, and certainly also to amend the Constitution of the Federation. Because in the blue book it was the representation of the autonomous provinces in the Federation bypassing the Republic of Serbia that was criticised. They were represented directly as if they were the subject of the Federation, whereas the 1974 constitution contained an express provision, stating that they did not have that property, they were not federal units; and yet they were represented in the Federation as if they were federal units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the amendments to the constitution of 1974, the federal constitution, that of the SFRY, when were they adopted?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The amendments to the constitution were adopted in two waves. The first time was when the principle of collective work, decision-making, and responsibility was established, and the second time was in 1988. So the SFRY constitution of 1974 was amended twice. The first time eight amendments were adopted, and on the second occasion there were about a dozen. I don't know the exact number, about a dozen amendments. There were quite a few amendments to the 1974 SFRY constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The amendments to the constitution of the SFRY, which were adopted in 1988, in relation to the situation described in the blue book was amended, or rather, the situation was amended, it was changed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by this expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the federal constitution was amended in order for it to be brought into line with the actual situation which was that these two autonomous provinces could not independently --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The amendments to the constitution of the Federation did not impinge on the constitutional position of the autonomous provinces within the Federation. The position of the autonomous provinces within the Republic of Serbia were changed in the amendments to the Constitution of Serbia in 1989, and these amendments were adopted after the federal constitution had been amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The amendments to the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia in 1989 were needed, and if I'm correct that this was recognised already in 1977, based on the conclusions in the blue book. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the blue book is an official document. It was not available to the public, but as for scholarly circles, scholars criticised these solutions severely from the point in time the amendments of 1971 were adopted to the 1963 SFRY constitution. And throughout the period in which the 1974 constitution was in force, scholars criticised sharply the position of the autonomous provinces in the constitutional system. A number of periodicals issued by the Faculty of Law in Belgrade in 1971 were banned because they contained criticism of the 1971 amendments, and these amendments laid down the main ideas on which the constitution of 1974 was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the amendments to the constitution of Serbia of 1989 referred in the same way, in an identical way, to the position of both autonomous provinces, Vojvodina and Kosovo, in the same way. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the position of the autonomous provinces had to be dealt with in a uniform manner. They don't have different statuses. They have exactly the same status, both within Serbia and within the Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, before the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia was amended, what changes had to be made to the Constitution of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The changes introduced in 1978 had to do primarily with the economic system, liberalizing the property regime, and they did not impinge on the status of the autonomous provinces within the Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'm interested in was what was -- what changes had to be made to the SFRY constitution before the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia could alter the state -- or could be amended to alter the status of the autonomous provinces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Constitution of the Republic of Serbia was changed to alter not just the status, but to redistribute the powers, the competences between the autonomous province and the republic. It did not go into the subject matter of the federal constitution, and the Serbian constitution could do that because it fell within the domain of the constitutional power of the Republic of Serbia. So even after the amendments of 1989, the autonomous provinces had exactly the same status within the Federation. There had only been a redistribution of powers between the provinces and the Republic of Serbia, and the most attention was paid and the greatest amount of criticism was levelled at the amendment which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a separate matter. Mr. Zecevic started this passage of his examination by putting it to you that what had to happen was that the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia had to be amended, and you corrected him and said that it was the SFRY constitution and the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia that had to be amended. I now understand you to be saying that anything that was done to affect the status of the autonomous provinces was exclusively in this instance within the competence of the Republic of Serbia, which is how he put it initially. Now, have I got that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, the Constitution of Serbia cannot regulate the status of the autonomous provinces in the Federation, because that is regulated by the federal constitution. The Constitution of Serbia on the other hand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you just stop there. Prior to 1989 were any amendments made in the Constitution of the Federation that affected the status of the autonomous provinces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, in these tabs somewhere you have the conclusions of the Federal Assembly of 1989 commenting on these amendments to the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia. So the federal organ, the Federal Assembly, commented on the constitutional changes in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'm just coming to that, so let's go step by step, please. Professor, adopting the amendments to the Constitution of Serbia was first done in both provinces and then in the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you now please look at tab 73, 1D751. These are the conclusions of the Federal Assembly of the SFRY of the 3rd of March, 1989, and, Professor, I have to explain, as we don't have a translation into English yet, it hasn't arrived yet, I just have to explain what this is about.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct you. The conclusions were made on the 1st of March, and they were published in the Official Gazette on the 3rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These conclusions were reached after the Presidency of the SFRY by its decision introduced special measures on the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo because of the unrest in that province in the course of February 1989. First let me ask you, according to the Constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the Presidency was authorised to introduce special measures on the territory of the SFRY. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was its constitutional power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These conclusions of the Assembly of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia of the 1st of March, as you indicated, refer precisely to these special measures introduced by a decision of the Presidency. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the preamble of this document, it says the following: "For the purpose of protecting the constitutional order, public law and order, personal security and the security of property, and the security and safety of all citizens and socially owned property, and the fastest possible normalising of the deteriorating situation in the socialist autonomous province of Kosovo, the Assembly of the SFRY, pursuant to Article 153, the rules of procedure," and I won't read the rest, "of the 1st of March, 1989, hereby adopts the following conclusion. "1. The Assembly of the SFRY supports the special measures, which the Presidency of the SFRY, within the scope of its constitutional competencies has taken, in order to preserve and protect the territorial integrity and constitutional order of the SFRY, to secure public law and order, the freedom to work and live, and to normalise the overall situation in the socialist autonomous province of Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, Your Honours, should I read all three paragraphs and then pose the questions or should I maybe ask Professor to comment on the paragraphs? It's just -- I'm just doing -- I'm reading this because of the -- we don't have a translation. That's -- that is the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These don't speak for themselves, they require comment, do they?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, some of them do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, if you can identify the parts that require comment and ask him about them, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, since we will eventually receive the translation and the Judges will be able to read the conclusions under 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9, I would like for you to comment the conclusion under item 10 of this document. 1 and 10, I apologise. So the one I have just read out and conclusion under item 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Professor, read conclusion 10, first of all, to us and then give us your comments on both number 1 and number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I should read, Your Honour, so it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter, but somebody should read 10 so that we know what it says, and then the Professor can comment on both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Conclusion under item 10: "The Assembly of the SFRY points out that the amendments to the SFRY constitution that have been carried out were aimed at enabling the implementation of the reforms of the economic and political system and that these amendments made no changes to the basic principles of the 1974 SFRY constitution. The Assembly of the SFRY believes that the adopted amendments to the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia, the amendments adopted by the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia, that these amendments provide the necessary unity and common spirit of all socialist self-management forces in Serbia which are in accordance with the positions taken at the 13th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. These amendments are important not only for the Socialist Republic of Serbia and socialist autonomous provinces, but also for ensuring the constitutional concept of the Yugoslav Federation and stability of the entire country and do not affect the status of the socialist autonomous provinces established by the Constitution of the SFRY. In order to ensure the necessary unity and common spirit or fellowship in the Socialist Republic of Serbia, the procedure of amending the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia needs to be concluded as soon as possible." End of item 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, would you please give us a brief comment of item 1 and item 10 of the conclusions of the 1st of March, 1989.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 1, the Assembly of the SFRY supports the special measures introduced by the Presidency of the SFRY, and they say that the Presidency has introduced those measures within its constitutional powers. This conclusion is especially important when one has in mind the nature of the then-existing constitutional system. At the time Yugoslavia was a socialist country. The principle of division of power was not in force there; rather, the unity of power was the principle applied, whereas the Assembly is defined in the constitution as the highest organ of power in accordance with the principle of the unity of power which existed in the then-Soviet Union and other socialist countries. So there is no division of power there, but rather unity of power. So the Assembly is defined as the highest organ of power and self-management. The importance of this support lies in the fact that it stems from the SFRY Assembly, that is to say the highest organ of power. This is what I have to say in relation to item 1. As for item 10, it presents the position of the SFRY Assembly. Once again, in its capacity as the highest organ of power. In its position in relation to the amendments to the SFRY constitution and the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, it says there that the amendments of the SFRY constitution, according to the conclusions taken by the Assembly, enable the implementation of the reforms of the economic and political system and that these reforms, even though fundamental, do not affect the basic principles of the 1974 constitution. And then, speaking of the amendments to the Serbian constitution, and they refer to the amendments to the constitution that we mentioned just a bit earlier, the 1989 amendments, they were passed by the Assembly of the SFRY, and the Assemblies of two autonomous provinces [as interpreted] had to express their agreement with them. If we put aside the ideological element, namely, that they were in line or in accordance with the positions taken at the 13th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, what is important from a legal point of view is that the Assembly says that these amendments do not affect the status of the socialist autonomous provinces established by the federal constitution. This means that the SFRY Assembly, as the highest organ of power, believes that the amendments to the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia of 1989 do not affect, do not change, in any way the position of the socialist autonomous provinces established by the constitution. This is why the SFRY Assembly refers, or rather, urges that the procedure for amending the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia be concluded as soon as possible. What remained to be done is that these -- that the Assemblies of two autonomous provinces expressed their approval of the amendments to the Serbian constitution, because that was the procedure for amending the Serbian constitution as established in its constitution of 1974.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the transcript, line 11 of that page, I think it should be the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would say Serbia, but we can ask Professor to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, when speaking of the amendments to the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, and you said that they referred to the amendments to the constitution that we mentioned just a bit earlier --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is as it should be because they referred to the -- yeah, it should be 1988 amendments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well you can't have it all ways, Mr. Zecevic, and it does need to be clarified. The way it reads at the moment is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you said: And then when speaking of the amendments to the Serbian constitution referring to the amendments to the constitution that we have explained just a bit earlier, that is to say 1989 amendments, they were adopted by the Assembly of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were adopted by the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, when you gave your comment on item ten of the conclusions, could one based on that conclude that in 1989 the amendments to the Constitution of Serbia did not infringe upon the autonomous rights of the autonomous provinces of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, that's correct. That's a very clear conclusion that the Assembly of the SFRY reached. They state that these amendments do not affect, do not change, the position of the socialist autonomous provinces established by the SFRY constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. That means that neither Kosovo nor Vojvodina were stripped of autonomy, but rather that a redistribution of competencies was done between the organs of autonomous provinces and the Republic of Serbia, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And those fell within the jurisdiction of the Republic of Serbia which had an equal status with other federal units within the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation, Professor. Could you now look at tab 5, please, P855, which is the Constitution of Serbia of 1990.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please comment Article 47 of the Constitution of Serbia; it deals with citizenship.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Article 47 deals with citizenship of the Republic of Serbia. "A citizen of the Republic of Serbia shall have citizenship of the Republic of Serbia. A citizen of the Republic of Serbia may not be deprived of his citizenship, exiled, or extradited." This means that there is a legal relationship between an individual and the state embodied in the citizenship, which grants protection to citizens. Then it follows on to say that: "Citizenship shall be acquired and terminated in the manner established by law," which means that it is not the constitution that regulates how a citizenship can be acquired and terminated. The constitution simply defines what citizenship is and what is the scope of protection granted to a citizen of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Could we now look at tab 6, please, which is P856, the translation is 1D139. This is the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Article 17, please. Were you able to find this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Constitution of FRY, Article 17. We saw earlier how the citizenship of the republic is regulated, but there was also the citizenship of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a dual citizenship that normally exists in a federation, that of the federation and of the federal unit. Based on the citizenship of the federal unit, each citizen is normally a citizen of a federation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 of Article 17 specifies precisely what I just said. Paragraph 3 indicates the scope of protection that of Yugoslav -- that a Yugoslav citizen enjoys, and we can see that that scope of protection is identical to the one that a citizen of Serbia enjoys. That is to say that a citizen of Yugoslavia cannot be deprived of his citizenship, deported from the country. In Serbia we had the word "exiled," and then a Yugoslav citizen cannot be extradited either. That's also contained in the Serbian constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Paragraph says that: "Yugoslav citizenship shall be regulated by federal law." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please go to tab 71, 1D226, this is the Law on Yugoslav citizenship, tab 71. Have you got that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the Law on Yugoslav Citizenship. We saw the paragraph of the constitution referring to this federal law. Article 1 says: "Yugoslav citizenship may be acquired in the following ways," and then it lists the conditions enshrined in this law?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is very much the same thing that the constitution suggests, how citizenship is acquired and how citizenship may cease and that is regulated by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Article 3 the possibilities are listed how citizenship may cease. Can you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are three textbook situations, if you like, one is release from citizenship, there is also the possibility of renunciation, and the third possibility is by international treaties. The important thing is that citizenship may cease or be revoked only if a person is already a citizen of another country, a foreign country, or at least if there is proof or certain indication that this person will acquire foreign citizenship. A person cannot be left without a home country and without citizenship just because his Yugoslav citizenship ceases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I want to know about something else. Both release and renunciation imply that the person in question must make an explicit request or statement in order to renounce from Yugoslav citizenship or be released from it. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that follows from Article 19 and Article 24 of this law. Citizenship cannot cease, cannot be revoked, without explicit request and without a Yugoslav citizen making this explicit request, submitting this explicit request, to be stripped of citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The third manner in which this may come about -- well, I don't think there is any need to comment on this now. This is by international treaty, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ratified and confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, bearing in mind what you have now told us, the fact that cessation of citizenship by renunciation or by release must be explicitly, unequivocally requested by the person in question. Well, there is one exception to this rule, paragraph 34 of this law -- Article 34. If you would please be so kind as to comment on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads: "Release from or renunciation of Yugoslav citizenship shall not be granted during a state of war within that is, a request -- no request shall be granted during a state of war or the imminent threat of war or a state of emergency." So while irregular circumstances prevail within Yugoslavia -- for as long as irregular circumstances prevail, Yugoslav citizenship shall continue in both these cases. We're talking about release and renunciation, and we have realised by now that these are the two basic modes for Yugoslav citizenship to cease.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The only third way seems to be by international treaty, right, so there are a total of three ways, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: International treaties are not something that this law is supposed to deal with. International treaties are international treaties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, if I understand you correctly, as far as Article 34 is concerned, even if there is an explicit request to renounce on Yugoslav citizenship, a person shall not be -- no person shall be granted this request during any of these three irregular situations, so to speak. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Professor, information concerning Yugoslav citizenship is kept in citizens' registers, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These books are public, and they are considered to be public documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So let's imagine the following situation. A Yugoslav citizen leaves Yugoslav territory, loses their ID papers, their passport, for example, or their passport is seized, let's try to assume that for a second, they do not lose their Yugoslav citizenship just because something like that happens, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they do not lose their citizenship. The same applies to an ordinary citizen, a man in the street, who simply loses his ID. He simply gets a new one issued. That's all there is to it. Passports are lost sometimes. Passports are lost all over the world on a daily basis. That doesn't mean that people cease to be citizens of their country. Citizenship can only cease on the conditions established in the relevant law. There are three such situations, as we have seen: Renunciation, release, and international treaty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. Let's now move on to something else, please. Could you please go to tab 9. This is the Constitution of the SFRY, it's the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is P1623.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One of the values enshrined in the constitution or that the constitution was based on was the idea of associated labour and the right of workers to self-management. Wasn't that crucial, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of the essential, crucial, features of the 1974 constitution. Its very name betrayed the social system that it stood for, I'm referring to the socialist. The country was called the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. One of the essential features, one of the milestones, of this system, this organisation, was precisely the subject of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Professor, if you could please briefly comment on Article 46 of the 1974 constitution. Just a minute, please. Let us try to depict this against a wider backdrop. The concept of property in the then-Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia placed socially owned property first, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the prevalent form of ownership, some sort of social monopoly, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So through the work of its various bodies, the state protected socially owned property, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Socially owned property and the right of workers to self-management were essential features of the economy of the then-Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. Can you please now briefly comment on Article 46.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article is part of a chapter of the constitution discussing the country's economy, economic set-up, its social and economic structure, if you like. What is at stake here is the preservation of these two fundamental values of the country's social and economic set-up. Article 46 is part of this chapter, and it must be interpreted in this context, against this background of specific articles and institutes. There is a mechanism that is described here that is used for the protection of the right of workers to self-management as well as the protection of socially owned property.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please comment on 129 and 139, Articles 129 and 139. These address the protection of socially owned property and the right of workers to self-management. This is, you might say, an elaboration of Article 46 of the constitution, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The basic principle of all these institutes is Article 129, paragraph 1 of Article 129 which reads: "The self-management rights of the working people and social property shall enjoy special social protection." Article 130, if you like, operationalises this form of social protection. "Organisations of self-management were the basic form of organisation in this sort of society. If in an organisation of associated labour another self-managing organisation or community self-management relations have become essentially disrupted or if serious harm has been caused to social interests or if an organisation community does not fulfil its statutorily established obligations, the assembly of the community socio-political shall have the right, and this is the Municipal Assembly under the rules, under condition and by procedures specified by Statute to dissolve the Workers' Council, which is the organ of self-management in this case, and call for new elections for the members of this body to dissolve in this organisation of associated labour self-managing organisation or community its executive bodies, and to recall the business boards, the individual business executive and workers holding executive posts nominate provisional bodies having statutorily defined rights and duties" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "or temporarily to" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, we can all read this when we've got other time to do it. It's your expert views that we're really seeking and just to clarify one thing, you're commenting on Articles 129 and 130 and not as said on line 22 and page 31 twice, Articles 129 and 139. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, have you a question on this, Mr. Zecevic, that you would care to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, based on this law there was particular state organ, the ombudsmen for self-management who would initiate proceedings in cases such as the ones we have just been reading about when they occur in a body of associated labour, and this is what Article 131 talks about, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is about the rights of self-managing workers and about socially owned property. This entire mechanism was established in order to be able to implement a principle from Article 10, which says that the entire economic system of Yugoslavia as a whole must be based on free associated labour and socially owned means of production and on self-management by the working people. So these are the two fundamental components expressing the very essence of how Yugoslavia was organised along economic lines: Socially owned property and self-management. 129, 130, and 131, these articles establish the basic mechanism for protecting these two fundamental values inherent to how the country was organised in a purely economic sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just very briefly, please, we only have five minutes left, tab 74. P1848, this is the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia, the relevant articles are 143 and 144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour, just to confirm that this is a completely the same as the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well that's not clear from what you've -- I assume that was the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but, Your Honour, this is a -- we need to establish because there is a federal level then the republican level, and then the level of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not the fact that you're going to another constitution I'm concerned about; it's focusing questions on it. It appeared as though you were simply inviting the Professor to read out Articles 143 and 144.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, I was not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was just laying down the foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, 142, 143, and 144, Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia. The title also contains the protection, self-managing protection of socially owned property. This is something that was taken from the federal constitution. There is no need to comment, really, because the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia had to be consistent with the Constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these solutions were simply taken over from the federal constitution, the solutions from the federal constitution were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order for these constitutional solutions to be implemented, there had to be laws envisaging ways to protect socially owned property and the modi and modalities of operationalised protection of socially owned property and the rights of workers to self-management. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what these laws were called.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at the oldest, or rather, the earliest of these laws? I'm talking about tab 75, 1D130. This is the law on temporary measures for the social protection of self-management rights and socially owned property. It was passed by the Assembly of the socialist autonomous province of Kosovo on the 27th December 1977. It was published in the Official Gazette of the socialist autonomous province of Kosovo on the 28th of December, 1977. The relevant articles are 1, 3, 8, and 25. However, Professor, all I am looking to elicit from you now is a very general comment. This law operationalises the constitutional protection of socially owned property and self-management rights of workers in the area of the autonomous province of Kosovo in 1977. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be a time -- it would be appropriate to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've reached the time for the break again, Professor, so could you please accompany the usher from the court, and he will again show you where to wait; and we shall resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we have looked at tab 75, 1D130. Now please turn to tab 76, that's 1D455. This is the law on amendments to the law on temporary measures to the social protection of the self-management rights and social ownership. The law was adopted by the Assembly of the socialist autonomous province of Kosovo at its session of the 30th of December, 1986, and it was promulgated in the Official Gazette, or rather, it was published in the Official Gazette of the socialist autonomous province of Kosovo, number 52 of the 31st of December, 1986. The articles we will be referring to are 1, 4, 7, 12, 14, and 20. I do not wish to go into the content of these articles. This law amends some provisions from the previous law we have looked at and mostly adds to them. This law was also adopted in order to make operational the protection of the constitutional values of socially owned property and the self-management rights of workers in the territory of Kosovo. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because Kosovo as an autonomous province had its independent legislative power and, just like the republic, it was duty-bound to further develop the institutes contained in the federal constitution. This was therefore done, both in the law and the amendments, these amendments we now see to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, both these laws, as we see from the Official Gazettes, were enacted by the Assembly of the socialist autonomous province of Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that was the only organ of the province that had legislative power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And both these pieces of legislation were enacted before the amendments to the Constitution of Serbia of 1989. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one can see that when one looks at the time-line, the chronology. This law was adopted in 1986 and the amendments were adopted in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But the previous law we were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was enacted as early as 1977, but you're asking me now about the law on amendments. The law on temporary measures for social protection of self-management rights and socially owned property was enacted in 1977, whereas the law on the amendments to that law were enacted in 1986 and in 1989 the Constitution of Serbia was amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So we may conclude that these two laws, the law of 1977 and the one of 1986, were enacted in accordance with the then-valid procedure which was in force at the time in compliance with the Constitution of the socialist autonomous province of Kosovo, with a view to implementing the provisions of the federal constitution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Could you now look at tab 78, 1D -- excuse me, please. I do apologise. Tab 76, we should take them in the proper order, 76 -- oh, sorry, we've seen that one. 78 then, 1D133. This is the same law, or rather, it's a law on provisional measures for the social protection of self-management rights and socially owned property of the socialist autonomous province of Vojvodina. It was enacted on the 21st of March, 1990, and published in the Official Gazette of the socialist autonomous province of Vojvodina, number 9, of the 31st of March, 1990. We will be referring to Articles 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, that's it, 2, 5, 6, 7, and 8. So I assume this is an identical case. A piece of legislation is being enacted in the Assembly of the province on the protection of institutions and values from the constitutional text, the constitution of federal state. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And finally tab 77, 1D458. This is the law on temporary measures for social protection of self-management rights and social ownership of the Republic of Serbia. And it was enacted by the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia and published in the Official Gazette of the Socialist Republic of Serbia, number 49, of the 28th of October, 1989. And we will be referring to Articles 1, 2, 8, 9, 11. This law was enacted by the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia now, with a view to implementing the provisions of the Constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia of 1974. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in all these laws, including the constitutional basis, the state by means of its organs is protecting social ownership and the self-management rights of workers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we have explained the reasons, because these were the foundations of the economic order of the whole country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The organ initiating these measures was the social attorney of self-management, and this organ existed at the republican level and likewise at the level of the socialist autonomous provinces?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in these laws we have seen the measures taken, the measures that you spoke about from the constitutional text implied dismissing the executive organs of companies, of management organs, the bringing of new persons, fresh persons to these positions, and so on?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These measures limited self-management because self-management had been violated, or rather, abused, as had socially owned property.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All these measures that were enacted, according to the text of the legislation had as their aim protecting the self-management rights of workers and socially owned property which was in the care of the state. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The purpose was not to discriminate or to be used as tools of discrimination of anybody; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only motive for taking these measures, as follows from the constitution and the legislation, is the protection of socially owned property and the self-management rights of workers using means of production which are socially owned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let's go back to the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia of the 28th of September, 1990, that's tab number 5, P855. At the very start of our conversation I think the day before yesterday, or Monday in any case, we spoke about the significance of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia of the 28th of September, 1990, which signified a break with the postulates of the previous constitution and the foundations of the then-social and economic system. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If that constitution of Serbia abolishes self-management, courts of associated labour, the leading role of the League of Communists, and introduces, or rather, puts all forms of ownership on an equal footing, guarantees private ownership, introduces a market economy, introduces a multi-party parliamentary democracy, a free market, the independence of the judiciary, and civil freedoms. I think I've listed everything more or less?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that constitution signified a radical break with the previous social and state order, and this was also expressed in the name of the Republic of Serbia. The ideological description of "socialist" was dropped and the state was simply called the "Republic of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Due to this change at the very beginning of our conversation on Monday, we mentioned that certain regulations ceased to be in force. Among the regulations which ceased to be in force are the ones we have just been talking about, those on the protection of social ownership and the self-management rights of workers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the simple reason that these were no longer categories in the constitution in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Also the organ of attorney of self-management stopped -- ceased to exist. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To illustrate this, please look at tab 79, 1D136. This is the law on the cessation of validity of the law on taking temporary measures for the social protection of self-management rights. Provisional measures for the social protection or self-management rights and socially owned property. And it lists, or rather, it states that on the 31st of December these measures and these regulations will no longer be valid, and this includes those of the socialist autonomous provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just need to add something to the transcript, page 41, 11, it's 31st of December, 1991, that is the date I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these laws we have been discussing were in force in Kosovo - I'm referring to the laws on the protection of socially owned property and the self-management rights of workers - they were in force from 1977 and then in 1986 they were amended. And as of the 31st of December, 1991, they -- their legal force was terminated?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that follows from Article 1.2, referring to Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the same case obtained -- the same thing obtained in the case of the regulations of the socialist autonomous province of Vojvodina in paragraph 3 and also similar legislation in the Republic of Serbia under point 1?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Article 2 it says that the provisional measures that had been taken pursuant to these laws shall be in force no longer than the 31st of December, 1991, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Unless the Assembly revoked them earlier?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The same goes for the provisional measures in relation to organisations and communities in the territory where special circumstances emerged. They were to cease to exist on the 31st of December, 1991, as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the territory where special circumstances arose was the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So all of these measures that we have just mentioned and that were discussed by a number of witnesses here ceased to be applicable as of the 31st of December, 1991, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that stems from Article 3 of this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we now please look at tab 80 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that. Professor, can we take it also that this is an illustration of one of the impacts of the amendment of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, so that the body now dealing with these measures in all three areas of the republic is the republic that's -- is the Serbian republic itself, and there's no longer jurisdiction in the provincial Assemblies to deal with these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This means that social property no longer enjoys special social protection - that was the reason why the special form of protection was established - but rather, that all types of ownership were put on an equal footing. The other element was that self-management was no longer a category of the 1990 constitution. So these two features of the economic order pursuant to the previous constitution ceased to exist in the 1990 constitution because that constitution introduced economic reforms, free markets, free entrepreneurship, and so on and these old features were no longer contained in the new constitution and they ceased to exist both in Serbia and in autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance Your Honour, because it is obvious that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I said if I may be of assistance, Your Honour, because it is obvious that Professor didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I understood that throughout the earlier part of this evidence the various laws you referred to were implementing the federal constitution, and now we have a situation where the provinces do not appear to be able to control this aspect of the law, it's a matter for the Republic of Serbia Assembly and not for their Assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did that just to save the time because if you remember I was referring to the federal constitution and then immediately after that to the Serbian constitution which had the very same provisions, Articles 142 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And we didn't went into that. So when they were implementing the federal -- the provisions of the federal constitution, they were automatically implementing the provisions of the Serbian constitution as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the body which had jurisdiction for the province of Kosovo to make this law, to implement the constitution, was the Kosovo Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now we're seeing that it's the Republic of Serbia Assembly which is recalling these orders so that must be because the constitutional amendment in 1990 removed from the Assembly of Kosovo the power to do this and put that power in the hands of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia. And I was seeking clarification of that. Now, the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness says that's not the case and perhaps he can explain it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, would you please explain this. Have you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand it this time around. Pursuant to the 1990 constitution, the provinces no longer had legislative power. They were able to issue decisions. Their Assemblies were able to issue decisions but no longer legislation, just like they no longer had power to adopt constitutions, they also no longer could adopt statutes as the highest legislative enactments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this satisfy it, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, tab 80, please, which is 1D137, and this is the Law on the Termination of Work of the Social Attorney for Self-Management, we're interested in Articles 1 and 5. This law terminates the organ that was meant to initiate procedures to protect social ownership and self-management rights of the workers, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in this particular case in Article 5, it says that this law will apply to the laws of Vojvodina and Kosovo, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the last item, tab 81, Professor, which is 1D138. This is the law amending, the law invalidating, the law on temporary measures for the social protection of self-management rights and social ownership or socially owned property. This law simply extends the deadline by which these laws were supposed to cease to be applied, so instead of the 31st of December, 1991, these laws that we have mentioned earlier were meant to cease to be applied by the 31st of December, 1992, correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So definitely after the 31st of December, 1992, there no longer was a possibility to introduce temporary measures in order to protect social ownership and self-management rights of the workers in the entire territory of Serbia, including autonomous provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has brought us to the end of the expert testimony of Professor Markovic.
