There is just one issue which Your Honour raised concerning the ministries -- concerning the ministries established in Serbia in 1991, this is at tab 17, 1D456. If I -- if I correctly remember, Your Honour was posing a question about why if, according to Professor, these were just so-called reserve authorities or reserve authorities of Republic of Serbia, why were the ministries, in fact, established in 1991 but ceased to exist by amendments of the Law on Ministries in 1993 after the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was brought up. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That related to the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry for International and economic development.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Three ministries which are within the competences of the federal state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I have done a research and maybe I can jog the memory of the Professor, if it pleases the Court, by just stating certain facts which might jog the memory of the Professor, and then he can give the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, do you remember the question put by His Honour Bonomy concerning the Laws on Ministries of the Republic of Serbia of the 5th of February, 1991, and later amendment to this law when these three ministries ceased to exist in 1993. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the Trial Chamber put a question inquiring why these ministries were established in Serbia if such ministries already existed at the level of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a federal state. I would like to ask you now, do you remember when the Republic of Slovenia held its plebiscite and declared its independence and sovereignty as a republic, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, I remember that. At the time I was a judge of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, and what they did was assessed in terms of its constitutionality by the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking too much, in view of my age. I can't remember the exact date, but I remember the event. As I said, I was a member on the Constitutional Court, and I know that we reviewed the constitutionality of this. As for the date, it's a difficult question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, 23rd of December, 1990, does this ring a bell? Could this possibly be the date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a whole series of enactments adopted by the Republic of Slovenia, and they were followed by enactments of Croatia. And they represented gradual secession from the Yugoslav Federation. All of those enactments were assessed for their constitutionality by the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Do you remember that also in December of 1990 Croatia -- the Republic of Croatia adopted its constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just as the Republic of Slovenia did in September of 1989, they adopted amendments to their constitution, and in it they established the priority of their constitution and laws in relation to those of the Federation. They said that in the territory of Slovenia the federal constitution and federal laws could be applied only if they were not contrary to the Constitution of Slovenia and laws of Slovenia. So they turned the principle upside down, the basic legal principle that is enshrined in every federation, which is the principle of the primacy of the federal law over the law of a federal unit. Slovenia did something that was quite contrary to that. They established the primacy of their law in relation to the law of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, at any rate these Slovenian constitutional amendments from 1989 were contrary to the solutions adopted in the SFRY constitution, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, and that was established in the decision of the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It wasn't clear in all of that what was the date of the adoption of the Slovenian constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, amendments to the Slovenian constitution that you just mentioned, which were in contravention of the federal constitution because they gave primacy to the Constitution of Slovenia over the federal constitution were from 1989?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, September of 1989. All of the republics, including the Republic of Serbia adopted amendments to their constitutions in 1989 because the Federation had amended its constitution in 1988 by way of amendments. So these amendments to the republican constitutions was a consequence of the fact that the federal constitution had been amended. And the republican constitutions had to be brought in compliance with the federal one. Slovenia used this opportunity to start gradual secession from the Federation, which was implemented through a series of enactments adopted by the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So these amendments were adopted Slovenia before the 1990 constitution was adopted by Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In December 1990, Croatia too, the Republic of Croatia, adopted its own constitution, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Both after and before on the 5th of October, on the 5th of October, 1990, Croatia passed a law on the structure of its republican administration, which is the equivalent of our Law on Ministries, thereby establishing its foreign office and its defence ministry, Ministry of Defence. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The ministries were set up in Serbia in February, or rather, a law was passed, 1D456, tab 17, the Law on Ministries that was adopted in February 1991 in the Republic of Serbia is a reflection of what occurred in Slovenia in 1989 and in Croatia in October 1990. These republics, likewise, had assumed the federal competences and applied them to their own republican level. They established their own state laws, you might say. Is that right, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So what we see here is some form of duality between the republican bodies on the one hand that were still operating in Slovenia and Croatia and afterwards in Serbia, and on the other the federal bodies start -- were not functioning but continued to exist and continued to do so until some time around April 1992, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There was a danger of secession and total disintegration in Yugoslavia, and the danger continued to exist until 1992 for as long as the 1974 constitution was still in power and until such time as the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted in 1992, April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After which, after which these ministries that we have mentioned, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defence, and the Ministry of Economic Relations with Foreign Countries ceased to exist in Serbia since they were under the jurisdiction of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Is that right, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following this, amendments were introduced to the Law on Ministries, establishing that these three ministries should cease to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is tab 18, 1D142, Official Gazette 1993, number 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if -- I hope this was sufficiently explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. We have one comment to make on exhibits so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Obviously we'll follow the practice that we've been following throughout the trial, which is to admit exhibits when they are introduced in some form in the trial to the extent that they are relevant to the evidence. And that will apply to any that you have referred to which are not already exhibits in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: However, there are at least two, I think, for which there were not translations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's pending, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But these will have to be identified at lunchtime today so that you can tell me exactly which they are, and we will specifically provide for them being subject to translation. They will not be admitted until the translation -- Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your -- definitely, Your Honour, I think I can do that even right now. It is document under the tab 19, 1D750.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which is a law on conducting foreign affairs within competencies of the federal administration organs and organisations, Official Gazette 56 of 1981, item 601; and the second one is the document under tab 73, 1D759 [sic] which are the conclusions of the Federal Assembly of SFRY, item 131, published in the Official Gazette of SFRY number 13 for year 1989. Those are the two documents which are -- I said -- it is just for the transcript it's 1D751, not 759, tab 73, 1D751, page 52, line 13 of the transcript says 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to make some submissions concerning some of the documents, but I too have to review my list. There are where I think there are only partial translations, and I may have an issue there. And there are one or two where, I think, where there's a question about provenance because they're not Official Gazettes. They're documents without a signature or a seal. There are more of those that relate to his factual evidence, I think, rather than his expert testimony so that will come, but I wanted to preview that for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's helpful but you can understand why it would have been quite neat to deal with the exhibits so far since we are now on to a different aspect of the evidence. So if it's possible after the break at midday for you to clarify whether any of the documents involved in the expert evidence are subject to what you've said, then we can clear this matter up hopefully. And until then, it's sufficient to mark for identification 1D750 and 751 and we have already done so in relation to IC133. Please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just bear with me one moment, please. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honours, if the binders have been distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, on the 5th of August this year you gave a 92 ter statement, which bears the following number 1D753, this statement is in relation to the facts and documents that you were presented with and listed in annex 1 of the statement. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're familiar with these facts and documents. In your statement you briefly explained each of the documents shown to you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your statement is truthful and is based on your knowledge and convictions. Were you asked the same questions about these documents again, you would provide identical answers in relation to each and every one of them, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would be seeking to ask that Professor's 92 ter statement, 1D751, be admitted, except -- 1D753, I'm sorry, be admitted except for the Politika newspaper documents, which I can list right now, which are -- which we are not seeking admittance of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggest that I follow the list which is in your binders or -- because the list which is attached -- the annex which is attached to the statement is a bit different. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's leave this and do it after lunchtime, if that's a simple way of doing it. You can present a list to the court deputy and we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- deal with it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, do your comments that you made a moment or two ago apply to some of the other documents referred to in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I think what I can do after lunch is advise you of the ones that I have a particular objection to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please continue for the moment, Mr. Zecevic, with any questions you have to ask about this document or any other matter, and we'll return to the formalities later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I appreciate it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you became a member of the cabinet of the Republic of Serbia back in 1994. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at tab 1, 1D385, the date is the 18th of March, 1994. This is a decision on the appointment of the president and vice-president of the Government of the Republic of Serbia and the republic's ministers. This was a government in which you were deputy prime minister in 1994, I'm talking about item 3, we see your name right there. Is that right, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was published in the Official Gazette, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a decision of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is because we were appointed by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. This document shows that you were deputy prime minister, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How many deputy prime ministers were there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a total of five deputy prime ministers, as you can see by reading this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, given the way the government was structured at the time, did each of the deputy prime ministers have special duties and responsibilities, different from those of other deputy prime ministers?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't ministers pure and proper. They had a direct relationship with the prime minister, and their duties and responsibilities were distributed by the prime minister. For example, I was in charge of legislation and the legal system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you stuck to that throughout your time in office, that's what Prime Minister Marijanovic had told you to do, and that's what you did from the moment you were appointed deputy prime minister to the termination of your time in office in 2000, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, first up until 1998 when this government was disbanded and then a new cabinet was appointed. Again I became deputy prime minister and again the government was headed by Mr. Marijanovic. I was given the same responsibilities in this new cabinet. I was in charge of legislation and the legal system of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. During the time of this second cabinet in 1998, in March 1998 more specifically, you were given a certain responsibility by the prime minister. Can you please explain specifically what this responsibility was about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, which tab should I be looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, try to think back and see if you can remember what the responsibility was.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which responsibility and what date?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: March 1998.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, back in March 1998 the prime minister, or Serbia's government if you like, gave me the responsibility of involving myself in talks with the leaders of Albanian parties and associations, or rather, I was tasked with heading a government delegation which included the following ministers: Ratomir Vico and Andrija Milosavljevic and Ivan Sedlak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you please look at tab 3, 1D078, this is an announcement made by the government on the 11th of March, 1998. It talks about a conclusion that was adopted on its session on the 10th of March. Is this what you have been talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is just it. This is an announcement which made public the substance of these conclusions. I headed this delegation of Serbia's government, the Government of the Republic of Serbia. The delegation comprised another three ministers, those that I've mentioned, and we were supposed to talk to the leaders of the Albanian parties. And this was about resolving certain practical matters concerning the life -- the everyday life of people in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, back in 1996 do you remember if the government set up a special group to implement the agreement on the return of Albanian pupils and teachers to schools in the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. The group was set up to have normalise teaching in schools and universities, to help normalise teaching in schools and universities, Ratomir Vico, Goran Percevic and Dobroslav Beletic were ministers who were involved in the work of this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please look at tab number 2 1D --, or rather, P714. This is the Official Gazette of the 12th of September, 1996. The document bears the number 933, it's a decision. Is that the decision you were referring to, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and it is precisely these members Ratomir Vico, who was a government minister; Goran Percevic, who was a federal deputy; and Mr. Dobroslav Beletic was a scholar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, when on the 10th of March you were tasked with, or rather, you were tasked by the prime minister of the Republic of Serbia, the late Mirko Marijanovic, with leading this delegation for negotiations with the Kosovo Albanians that you talked about, had you ever dealt with these issues before that point in time? I mean talks with the Albanian leaders about solving the issues of the continued functioning of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never before that had I been given any tasks connected to Kosovo and Metohija. This was the first time I was given a task in that connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, at this point in time, are you aware that any kind of negotiations took place between the leaders of the Kosovo Albanians and some members of some political parties in Serbia in the course of 1996 and 1997?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what talks you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were appointed to chair that delegation, were you aware that any kind of talks were being conducted with the leaders of the Kosovo Albanians in 1996 and 1997?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in any such talks. As I said, the first time I was given such a task was on the 10th of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But had you heard about any such talks?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably there were talks of that kind because Kosovo and Metohija was an area which was in political terms very full of unrest, ever since the early 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you know a certain person called Mr. Tanic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard about him in the media. He was very prominent. I think he was the spokesman of a political party, the Civic Alliance and especially New Democracy. I met him only once when we had lunch with the German ambassador, the ambassador of Great Britain was also present at that lunch hosted by the German ambassador. And that was my only physical contact with him. I saw him once in person. Before that I had seen him on television because he was very prominent in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you ever participate in any negotiations with the Kosovo Albanians together with Mr. Tanic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, no, never. He was never given any tasks by the government. He was not a public official, and I repeat I met him physically only once when the German Ambassador, Mr. Gruber, invited us to lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you never consulted him about negotiations or anything like that, that you coordinated positions with him?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, why would I? I never had any kind of contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, after you were appointed the leader of that delegation on the 10th of March, 1998, what steps did you take? What did that delegation of the Government of the Republic of Serbia do first?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first that delegation convened a meeting in Pristina, or rather, it scheduled a meeting and it was supposed to meet representatives of the Kosovo Albanians, thus opening the so-called political process and begin solving the issues affecting the daily life of citizens in Kosovo and Metohija. The meeting was scheduled. A public announcement was issued. Invitations were sent out to the private addresses of the leaders of the Albanian political parties, and I think it was supposed to be on the 12th of March, 1998. However, they never showed up at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just go slowly. So, Professor, the first meeting you scheduled was on the 12th of March, 1998, in Pristina. You arrived but they did not show up?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The delegation arrived, but I have to say that at the time that this delegation was being established, the government called on every party in the National Assembly to give one representative from their group of deputies to participate in these talks, with a view to affirming the unified approach of the National Assembly to the solution of issues in Kosovo and Metohija. The community of Hungarians from Vojvodina responded, and they sent their representative so that this gentleman went there together with the government delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Professor, the reason for this government communique, which we saw in tab 3, 1D078, of the 11th of March, and the decision of the prime minister to appoint you and your other three colleagues to this delegation was motivated to the best of your knowledge by what?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the course of my research I had dealt for a long time with issues of territorial autonomy in the world, and I have published many papers on that topic. I studied especially autonomy in Italy and Spain, the then-USSR, so that probably it was because I had a scholarly interest in the subject matter of territorial autonomy, and I knew the subject. Mr. Andrija Milosavljevic and Ratomir Vico were conversant with the conditions of living in Kosovo and Metohija. Mr. Vico was a minister who had already been tasked with conducting negotiations about normalising teaching in Kosovo and Metohija and Mr. Sedlak who was himself a member of a national minority was the minister in charge of human and minority rights in the Government of the Republic of Serbia. And I'm sure that this was the motive why the prime minister proposed this team to negotiate with the Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Professor, thank you for your response, but I wanted to know what the motivation of the cabinet was, of the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean for the negotiations themselves, well that was to find a peaceful way through political negotiations, to solve the problems on Kosovo and Metohija, because at that time armed conflict was already escalating in Kosovo and Metohija and this was an offer to solve everything in a civilised, peaceful manner through political negotiations of all the interested subjects. The international community had also appealed to the Republic of Serbia to act in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, if I understood you correctly, the government's policy was to take political measures, to engage in negotiations, in order to solve the situation in Kosovo at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One can see that from the persistent attempts made by this delegation, even at the cost of physical maltreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we went there dozens of times. We persistently attempted to have the whole matter discussed in a peaceful, political way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, that was the position of the government in March 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 10th of March, 1998, in the first half of March 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You were the deputy prime minister until the year 2000. This political standpoint of the government, was it ever changed in that period?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This position, this standpoint of the government, was not changed. This is also evident from the fact that the government, and later on the National Assembly, agreed to the negotiations in Rambouillet and in Paris and the government appointed a state delegation to negotiate in Rambouillet and Paris. The government always gave priority to political means for the solution of burning issues, issues of daily life in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time -- oh, I'm sorry. I'm obviously anxious to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, after you went to that meeting on the 12th of March where the delegation of the Albanian representatives did not show up, did you go there again on the next day, the 13th of March?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we went there on the following day. I looked it up, and those were -- those days were Thursday and Friday of that week. And then on the following week we went on every working day, and we scheduled the meeting in the same place at the same time every day and informed the leaders of the Albanian political parties. This was in Pristina, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you went there on the 12th and the 13th, which were a Thursday and a Friday, and then on the following Monday, the 16th, and from that time on you went there every day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I even recall the address, Vidovdanska 2, because I had gone there so many times, but every time the leaders of the Albanian political parties failed to turn up at those meetings, they failed to show up for them. Later on there were representatives of other ethnic communities who participated in that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, just take it easy, we'll go in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, do you remember the declaration of the President of the Republic of Serbia of the 18th of March, 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and that declaration was made in order to encourage political dialogue, to support a peaceful and political solution of the problems in Kosovo and Metohija. So apart from the government calling for negotiations and also the president of the republic called on the representatives of the Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija to participate in these talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please look at tab 5, 1D079.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the declaration you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it says in paragraph 2: "I appeal to the leaders of the political parties of the Albanian national minority in Kosovo and Metohija to start a political dialogue without delay and without conditions and as the president of the Republic of Serbia, I'm willing to be the guarantor of such talks on the basis of territorial integrity and sovereignty and Kosovo and Metohija within the framework of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, Professor, how do you understand this willingness of the president to guarantee the talks between your delegation and the representatives of the Albanian minority and the delegation of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was just waiting for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understood it as follows. The president of the republic guaranteed that whatever was agreed would be implemented. And as this declaration is a rather extensive text, it states what the president of the republic expects from these talks. It says that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is a European country committed to European values and principles, that he is convinced that the future of the citizens in Kosovo and Metohija is not an ethnic, religious, and cultural division and isolation, but in mutual linking up and living together. So the president expressed the spirit in which these talks should be conducted, and he expressed his willingness to guarantee the implementation of whatever was agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, you told us yesterday about the very limited powers of the president. Under what power would he be able to guarantee the success of the talks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is not really a power. This is a moral position that he took. The president of the republic, who was elected directly by all of the citizens, guaranteed that the agreement would be implemented. He represents the state of Serbia and symbolises its unity, and it is in this capacity that he spoke. Naturally, he did not have any specific powers in relation to this. This is all on the -- was said on the moral grounds. The negotiations were of political nature. It was the representatives of government and leaders of Albanian political parties that negotiated. There were no state organs involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, upon the return from Pristina on the 20th, on those seven occasions when you went to meetings starting on the 12th, none of the Albanian representatives showed up, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only two members of Albanians ethnic community showed up, but they were not leaders, they were not members of the majority political parties. Those were Mr. Faik Jashari and Mr. Sokol Qusha. However, they were not members of these majority political parties who had the support of the majority of Albanian citizens, members of the Albanian ethnic community, rather they were leaders of smaller political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you're referring to leaders of larger political parties, you are primarily referring to the late Dr. Rugova?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. They had the dominant position in the political life in Kosovo at the time. That was the dominant political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 6, 5909 [as interpreted], is the decision that you have already mentioned. This is the second cabinet where you served as deputy prime minister and Mirko Marijanovic once again was the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in that government I had the same tasks as in the previous government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's document 1D909.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, P909, P909.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's been recorded as 5909 but it's P.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, P909. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, on the 31st of March there was a declaration or a statement issued by the government on Kosovo, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's tab 8, 1D082. Could you please comment on this government appeal. As far as I can see, this is again an appeal to Albanian leaders to come to the meetings and negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a repeated call issued by the government after a series of unsuccessful trips of the members of its delegation. They're stating here that in the world the declaration of the president of Serbia was welcomed, and once again they issue a public appeal to hold a direct and unconditional dialogue with the representatives of all ethnic minorities. Because other ethnic minorities other than Albanian also asked to be involved in this political process. It says there that an indispensable method of resolving all issues in Kosovo and Metohija was the method of applying political mechanisms in order to achieve European standards on human rights and freedoms but also to respect the rights and freedoms of ethnic minorities. And here the government elaborates on its views concerning these talks. This is a somewhat longer statement of the government. If it's been translated into English, there's no need for me to convey the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Professor, did you start sending out written invitations, written notices, to attend to the Albanian leaders?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In order for them not to use a pretext or an excuse that this was a public invitation and not an invitation sent to private residences, then letters were also sent containing invitations to private addresses; namely, to Ibrahim Rugova, Demaqi, Krasniqi, and some others. A number of persons, all of them listed in this statement in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a correction, by your leave. It says here: "The composition of the delegation." Given that the cabinet had some changes, this is March of 1998 and there were some changes in the cabinet, and they were reflected in the composition of the delegation as well, meaning that Professor Milovan Bojic as a deputy prime minister was included, as was Mr. Tomislav Nikolic, also deputy prime minister. And Mr. Milosavljevic Sedlak and myself were there just like we were previously. As for the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, he appointed his special representative, and that was deputy prime minister of the federal government, Professor Vladan Kutlesic. So the delegation was expanded significantly, and in addition to the delegation there was also a Special Envoy of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just another question, Professor, before we break. Professor Vladan Kutlesic was who, if you can just tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Vladan Kutlesic at the time was deputy prime minister of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And he's a professor of what?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on he became, and today he's -- actually today he's no longer, but he became professor at the Faculty of Political Sciences, and recently he changed his job and now teaches at the Megatrend University.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time now, so again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Time now for the lunch break, Professor. Could you again please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will see you in an hour at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it was the wish of the Trial Chamber to deal with the -- to deal with 1D753, the Rule 92 ter statement of Professor Markovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, first -- yeah -- well, Mr. Hannis said he would make certain submissions about this which we can look at, but one thing you said you would do is clear up --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the question of the Politika articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We will not be seeking to tender the paragraph 17 of the statement of Professor Markovic. Paragraph 17 is on the page 12 -- it starts on the page 12 and continues until page 13. And all the Politikas are listed there, except 1D046 which is Politika of 19th November, which by mistake is included in this list, but it's already been admitted previously during the Prosecution case through Witness Petritsch. So this document has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you don't need to have it admitted again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. We will use the original --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. And all others listed under the paragraph 17 we will not be seeking to tender these into the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to be referring at all in the oral examination of Mr. Markovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to any of these?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And so far as the -- well, I better hear from Mr. Hannis first of all. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- having gone through the list now, a number of items that I had marked as having some concerns about from the original 65 ter notification are not on the list, so pretty much all of my problem exhibits have gone away. I don't know if we mentioned Exhibit 1D748 which is number 80 on the list of fact exhibits with the red binders, which is still pending translation, that's the only issue I have with that one. And I think we've addressed all the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the rule is clear that even if a document is referred to in evidence but has not been translated into English, it will not be admitted unless it's specifically raised, for example, on the basis that enough is translated in the course of the interpretation here for it to be unnecessary for any more translation to be done on it. But in the absence of that sort of determination, it's up to the party presenting it to get it into English before it will be admitted. What exactly is annex A, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Annex A is a list of all the documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this just the index for the binders?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's just the index for the binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are the ones being referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, that's right. And actually, his 92 ter statement has 17 paragraphs, and we are not seeking to tender the paragraph 17, which is referred to on page 12 and 13 of his 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, what's effectively being done here is the incorporation into the oral evidence of Professor Markovic of all these documents other than those referred to in paragraph 17, all those documents which are mentioned in his 92 ter statement. I take it that on the face of it they look authentic as far as you're concerned, and in the end of the day it's all going to be a question of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. So far as the documents referred to in his evidence as an expert are concerned, there are no others that you have any concern about, apart from the three which had not been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, Your Honour. So I was going through making notes when he testified, and looking at the list I don't think there was anything. There are a couple I have questions about, but I don't have questions about authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that situation -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Your Honour, but there is one other issue I think I should raise with the Trial Chamber or actually inform the Trial Chamber about. It's at tab 63 of the laws and regulations exhibits. It's the Law on VJ, P984, which we have a problem with Article 4 on the paragraphs, is it a paragraph 2 or 3 or 1 and so. And we have produced today the web site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I understood the reaction by my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, from the Office of the Prosecutor that he might be having an issue with that. So what we have done in the meantime is we have contacted the legal committee of the National Assembly of Serbia, which is the only body or organ that can provide with the authentic explanation of all the laws which have been brought up in the National Assembly. However, due to vacation issue, they will not be meeting before the 25th of August. So I would assume that after the 25th of August we will have an official explanation on the Law on VJ and the particular Article 4 that we are having here as an issue by the -- or legal committee of the National Assembly of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that IC exhibit will remain marked for identification until you make a joint submission filing --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to the Trial Chamber, or in the event of you being unable to make a joint one that you raise it because the onus will be on you to remove it from that status.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Thank you very much. I just wanted to inform the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in these circumstances, the general rule we've applied will apply to all the exhibits that have been referred to in the course of the evidence so far by Professor Markovic. They will be admitted to the extent that they are relevant to issues raised in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we please have the witness back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, how are you feeling?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe you on that one. Professor, about the declaration of the Government of Serbia concerning Kosovo dated the 31st of March, 1998, we spoke about that. Do you remember Resolution 1160 of the Security Council of that date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at tab 9, P0455.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, would you please go slowly because we have been asked by the interpreters to wait for the document to appear on the screen before commenting on it. Professor, see on page 1 we have Resolution 1160, which notes the declaration of the president of Serbia, or rather, the declaration of the president of Serbia on the situation in Kosovo. On page 2, the Security Council invites sides, that is to say Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and leadership of the Kosovo Albanians, to do certain things and to undertake certain measures, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please give a brief comment to items 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8 of the resolution in light of -- in light of what the Government of Serbia did up until the 31st of March when you were appointed a member of that delegation for negotiations, so what the government did before this resolution was issued, just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this resolution, the Security Council calls upon the government in Belgrade to offer a true political dialogue to the leadership of Kosovo Albanians. This resolution was adopted on the 31st of March, 1998, and the government in Belgrade had offered a political dialogue to them prior to that, back on the 10th of March. And on the 12th we already travelled to Pristina. It is further stated here that a political solution to the issue of Kosovo through dialogue without an alternative, then they call upon the leadership of the Kosovo Albanians to condemn all terrorist action. Then they welcome the decision to implement the agreement on education. We spoke about that agreement. Back in 1996 the government had established a negotiating team. Then they call upon all countries in order to establish peace and stability in Kosovo to either stop or prevent any shipment of arms to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, including Kosovo and its citizens from their territory. So everything that this resolution mentioned is something that the Government of Serbia had already done. What is also important for me, looking at this resolution, is the qualification given in the preamble, where it says that they condemn all terrorist operations on the part of the KLA. So from the highest international forum there was a message sent about the KLA using terrorist methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, the text of the resolution and what the resolution invites parties to do and what it requires parties to do is something that the Government of Serbia had already been doing two weeks before the resolution was issued, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, following that in April you travelled to Kosovo several times again, attempting to meet with the leadership of Kosovo Albanians, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Professor, whether you travelled to Pristina on the 7th of April for talks there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went on the 7th of April as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of April, was it the entire delegation that travelled or how was it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milan Milutinovic, travelled on the 7th as well as the entire delegation established by the Government of Serbia, again with the same objective. We believed that such a strengthened delegation of Serbia would perhaps produce a better response among the leaders of Kosovo Albanians, the leaders of political parties, and that this would give an impetus to political dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you remember that on that occasion President Milutinovic gave a statement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at tab 10, which is 1D083.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have that document in e-court, please. 1D83.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, is this the statement we have just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the statement issued by President Milutinovic on the 7th of April, 1998, in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please read the last line of the first paragraph, which begins with: "Coming here today ..."

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Coming here today, I wanted to underline the significance we attach to such talks."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain what is meant here.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said in the answer to the last question, as the delegation had now been strengthened with the arrival of the president of the Republic of Serbia, it was thought that this would be an impetus, that it would encourage the leaders of the -- the political leaders of the Albanians to respond to the invitation to talks. And the president, who according to the constitution, personifies the republic, embodies state unify, is here underlying the significance attached to these talks, demonstrating that the official state of Serbia seriously wants talks. So not only are representatives of the government present, but also the president of the republic. And this testifies to the fact that Serbia seriously wants talks because it's sending its highest state official to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In his statement the president repeats a wish -- in fact, he repeats his position, saying that the future of Kosovo does not lie in closing up and division, but on the contrary, in openness. And he expresses his dissatisfaction with the fact that the Albanian representatives have again failed to show up. Is that correct, that they failed to show up?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not show up, and in spite of the fact that there was such a strong delegation which had been ignored, the president points out that -- that Serbia remains willing to engage in dialogue, and he is willing to meet them at any time in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What notice was given to the Albanians of the meeting on the 7th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were always notified, from the time when they complained that the invitations were not arriving at their home addresses but that they were being invited only through public announcement. From that point in time onwards, they were always invited personally and the invitations were sent out to their home addresses. The list of invitees has just been mentioned. It's a broad circle of Albanian political leaders whom we mentioned before the break, and they received not only this general public invitation, but also personal invitations sent to their home addresses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you any idea when the invitation was made, both publicly and privately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't answer that because it's a technical issue I did not deal with, but I believe the invitations were sent out in time. The town is in the same country. It doesn't take so long for the post office to do its job, and probably there was a secure mechanism of delivering these invitations. I know that there had to be signatures, they had to sign receipts that they had received the invitation, especially Mr. Rugova, he had to sign receipts every time, or rather, his Chief of Staff had to sign a receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it that you're speculating about how the personal invitations might have been delivered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not speculating, because Mr. Veljko Odalovic showed me a receipt signed by the chief of Mr. Rugova's cabinet, Mr. Merovci, a receipt stating that he had received the invitation. Mr. Veljko Odalovic showed me that signed receipt. However, as head of the delegation, I was not in charge of these technical matters. So I don't know what method was used to send out the invitations. It was my job to -- to direct the talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your suggestion is, though, that it was done by the post office, and I wondered whether that was speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the technology was, I don't know, what the method was used -- what method was used, whether they were sent by post, through the post office, or some other methods, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, very briefly, I would like to take you back to tab 8, 1D82. This is a statement of the Government of the Republic of Serbia on Kosovo and Metohija. Page 2, the last two paragraphs, which I think explain what technical methods were used to send out the invitations.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the statement of the 31st of March, 1998, the representatives of the political parties of the Albanian minority are invited to attend a meeting seven days from today. That was the 7th of April, 1998, in Pristina in Vidovdanska number 2, the building of the republican government at 1200 hours. So seven days before the meeting was scheduled, they knew there was to be a meeting, but in addition to this public invitation the Government of Serbia sent out written invitations to the representatives of the political parties of the Albanian minority and public personalities, and then they list all the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have your answer. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, talking about letters, after the 7th of April did you go to Pristina an another occasion in April?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the specific date. I'm afraid I might be wrong if I try to tell you the date, but in April, May, and August we went there to have meetings with Mr. Fehmi Agani who failed to show up yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you remember whether you went to Pristina on the 16th of April, 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And none of the Albanian representatives showed up; although as you said, they had been informed both by public and written invitations about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both public and private, personal, invitations. I signed those invitations. I signed those invitations to all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene. Forgive me for interruption. Now, obviously these were very seriously meetings and were also asquel [phoen] to what the Security Council had stated. Was it enough to send these letters through transmissions by post? Because usually people intervene. There are mediators, there are people who try to bring parties together, and they are put in for purposes of persuasions and calling people for meetings. Is it in your knowledge, sir, that such method was employed or was it just perfunctory sending notices as it was being suggested through the post office only? That is what I thought if you would like to say anything on this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say once more I'm not sure the post office was used, it's just my assumption. But possibly it was not sent through the post office. Possibly all these invitations were sent through Mr. Veljko Odalovic, and he may have delivered those letters personally to the addressees through his people. I don't know what the methods, physical methods, of delivering the letters were. But if somebody is sent a polite invitation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, we know your position on this. What the question relates to is quite a different matter, and that is whether in the context of this important issue, you wouldn't expect some mediator, negotiator, or some intermediary to be acting to arrange the meeting rather than you as the leader of the delegation deciding when the meeting would be, sending out these invitations, and expecting everybody to turn up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know what intermediaries you mean. These are people who live in the same country. They lived in one and the same country. Pristina is in the Republic of Serbia. Albanians were citizens of the Republic of Serbia. So what sort of intermediaries would be needed? I don't understand. The government and the president of the republic were going there to meet them. They could have proposed a place and a time that suited them, but evidently it was their intention not to talk directly without intermediaries to the Government of the Republic of Serbia and its delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Yes, learned Professor, you had signed the invitations, you had gone there also. And then when they didn't show up, did you thinker of bothering to inquire whether things were served, whether somebody should be sent to them as an emissary? Obviously they were a different group. Within the same countries people negotiate through intermediaries or to emissaries or special messengers or common friends. It's not that people do it only in the international arena, it's also within. Even in the same house, somebody comes in. So I was wondering why this sort of attitude was shown, nobody bothered to check or remind them or persuade them or send somebody to them. After all, this was a very important matter, and what I hear from this declaration, this statement of the president, he was all serious about it. Then somebody had to implement this then. Why wasn't it done and nobody cared whether they were coming or not, who was served, who did not serve, what further steps be taken. Was all this a perfunctory exercise or a meaningful is a question which would arise in our mind, and we shall be grateful if you very kindly throw some light on it because you were the actor, the main participant, and nobody else will be able to tell us this. I'm grateful for your patience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there is testimony by Mr. Fehmi Agani that they always received those invitations, but that they deliberately did not want to respond to them. So it was not a matter of the technology of delivery and the physical receipt of the invitations, but rather of a political standpoint that they did not want to attend these meetings because that would amount to an admission that Kosovo and Metohija was a part of the Republic of Serbia. It would be tantamount to a recognition of the Republic of Serbia. Therefore, the issue was not that they had not received the invitations, but that it was their firm standpoint that they would not attend those talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, although that doesn't answer the question, I think we should move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, you said you signed invitations and notices. How many days' notice would have been under those invitations and those notices? That's my first question. Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that can be seen from the government statement. It was done seven days in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My next question to you is this: In the normal course of things, if you post a correspondence or a letter, such as your notice or invitation, from the destination where these would have been posted, how long would it have taken in the post to get to the varied destinations that the notices were sent out to? That's another question I wanted to know. In the post or via the post.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, according to my personal experience, you would receive it the next day after it was posted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And other than the post, in the system that was being employed for delivery of notices for those that were not -- if they weren't posted, how long would your internal delivery system take to make delivery of correspondence, as a general rule? Is it that it would remain in the system for a few days or would there normally be immediate delivery or how would it be carried out? If you don't know, you can say you do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think I can remember what happened. The chief of the Kosovo district was Mr. Veljko Odalovic. I think that the invitations were sent to him, and he with his team personally organised the delivery of the invitations to the addresses of the invitees. I know that Mr. Odalovic showed me the signature of Mr. Rugova's chief of cabinet, confirming receipt of the invitation, but I don't have it with me of course now. Mr. Odalovic may still have it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor Markovic. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you sent these letters to everyone that they were addressed to in the same way, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the very same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, some of them turned up. I think you mentioned two specific names of members of some Albanian political parties, but not the key Albanian political parties. So two minor politicians responded to these invitations.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best illustration of the fact that the invitations were received was the fact that Mr. Faik Jashari and Mr. Sokol Qausha regularly turned up. The same could be said of the representatives of the Roma national minority and the Egyptian national minority as well as the Turks, Guber Hasabovic [phoen] and Zenel Abedin Kures [phoen]. The same thing applies to the representatives of the Gorani, they all received their invitations and they all turned up for the meeting, which means that there was nothing wrong with the delivery system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. Do you remember if you personally sent a letter in April 1998 to Ibrahim Rugova?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I did send a letter to Ibrahim Rugova and Fehmi Agani.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd be hard-put to remember the exact date, but one thing that I do know for certain is I sent letters to those persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the letters were about, letters that you sent to Mr. Rugova and Mr. Fehmi Agani?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Might I be shown the letters before I start commenting? It's very difficult to keep all of these things in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is tab 11, 1D18, 3, 4, and 9, the page in e-court is 349, this is paragraph 6, your letter dated the 26th of April, 1998, do you recognise it sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, it's quite an extensive letter that I sent to Mr. Rugova. I outlined the basic elements for talks, for a dialogue. I restate my conviction, which was that of the state of Serbia as well, that violence is not acceptable for achieving -- is not a viable tool for achieving political aims. I also specify what I believe this dialogue should comprise, the dialogue between the state delegation and the representatives of all national minorities, all ethnic minorities, in Kosovo and Metohija, including, needless to say, the majority Albanian community. There is an English translation; therefore, I will not now recount the substance of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this letter, Professor, you refer to a meeting that was scheduled for the 28th of April, the 28th of April, 1998. Is that not right, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was precisely what I proposed to Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the 28th of April, 1998, in Pristina. What about that meeting, did the representatives of the Albanian party turn up?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 28th of April, if memory still serves -- well, I can't remember. There were 16 or 17 such invitations and futile visits to Pristina on our part. It wasn't more than once that we managed to meet representatives of the Albanian political parties. It was in the headquarters of the Kosovo and Metohija literary association, writers' association, and the talks were headed for the Albanians by Fehmi Agani and by myself on behalf of the Serb side. I'm afraid I might get the dates wrong, but we did go 16 or 17 times to meet them. And it wasn't but once that we managed to actually meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about the date of the 22nd of May, the headquarters of the Pristina writers' association, does that ring a bell, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was in May. I do remember that. There were a large number of foreign and domestic journalists from all sorts of media. It was more a ceremonial meeting. These were no substantial talks between the two parties. At the same time, this was the one and only time we ever met during all of these efforts that we made to open a political dialogue to have a proper political dialogue with the representatives of the Albanian community.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you said that the meeting took place on the 22nd of May, was attended by the late Fehmi Agani. Do you remember who else was there on behalf of the Albanian side?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Veton Surroi, Blerim Shala, Mahmut Bakalli, Mr. Kelmendi, these are some of the persons I remember as being there, but you must bear in mind the fact that this was all nine years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. Do you remember the meeting between President Milosevic and President Yeltsin in Moscow in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that a declaration, a joint declaration, was announced that resulted from that meeting -- that was reached at that meeting. It was signed in Moscow, and all I remember is what I read about this in the media. I wasn't personally involved in this meeting in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the substance of the joint declaration signed by President Yeltsin and President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember the substance. It reflected the positions of our government. It prioritized a peaceful solution for resolving open issues by political means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This declaration lifted any sort of restriction on diplomatic emissaries of foreign countries in terms of their diplomatic contacts in Kosovo. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the requests that were made in that declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Unhindered access was guaranteed to all of Kosovo's different areas to humanitarian organisations, including the International Red Cross. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the things stated in the declaration. I do remember that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Most importantly, do you remember that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia expressed its readiness to welcome OSCE to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, we have now conducted a brief analysis of the substance of this declaration. In essence, did it reflect the position and the policies pursued by Serbia's government at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflected not only the policies and the position of the government, but of all the political players in Serbia at the time. This was a position that had been agreed upon by all in sundry in Serbia. Everyone believed that this was the only way to go about all these open issues in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you remember that you wrote a letter to Fehmi Agani in August?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in August that I called on Mr. Fehmi Agani to attend talks, the intention behind this being I wanted to try talking to a specific person. We were colleagues. He was a university professor as well as I was, and I believed that a sense of academic solidarity between the two, especially since I was the one going to Pristina, that would prompt Mr. Agani to respond to my invitation and to have an informal talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you please go to tab 17, 1D061. Is this the letter that you wrote and is this the public announcement that you made subsequently, the letter you wrote to Professor Agani as tab 17?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. On page 1 you can see exactly what I was asked before, what the channels were for sending in signatures. This was the information stated, the name of the sender, the reference, when the letter was received or an invitation. On the previous page Mr. Fehmi Agani says explicitly: "We received your letter" -- no, I'm just trying to answer the question that I was asked before, when I was unable to state anything with certainty. So the letters were received.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let us please take this one step at a time. There are a number of technical matters that we need to resolve now. This is one of those documents that we have no English translation for. Please try to focus on your letter dated the 17th of August, 1998. Could you please read it and --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter is a simple one. I address him as: "Dear Professor Agani," as a gesture of solidarity. "In relation to your letter dated the 17th of August this year, I am glad to be able to express my satisfaction that you, too, want our talks to resume as soon as possible. Let it be that way. "Therefore, I propose that we meet as soon as tomorrow, Tuesday, the 18th of August, at 1400 hours, in Pristina at Vidovdanska Street number 2. I'm expecting your reply. Sincerely," on behalf of Serbia's government, I signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that's your letter?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my letter and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you turn to the next page, there is a public announcement which contains the text of the letter which you have just read back to us, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you invoke here a letter sent to you by Professor Agani. Can you please go to tab 16, 1D064. We do have a translation for this one.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered this letter that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I scheduled talks for the next day. I was the one who travelled from Belgrade to Pristina. Mr. Agani was in Pristina already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor in his letter -- Professor Agani talks about the mediation of Ambassador Hill, who is in constant contact with both Belgrade and Pristina. That's what Mr. Agani claims in the very last sentence of the letter?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about your letter written on that same day, what about your agreement to meet him? Does that not indicate that you had absolutely no problem whatsoever with the fact that this meeting should be mediated by ambassador --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, please, it's a very leading question. We're now into matters of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
