utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, what was your position regarding this proposal made by Mr. Agani in his letter dated the 17th of August?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I welcomed his initiative to have talks. I also proposed for us to meet the next day in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your letter you made no mention of Ambassador Hill's mediation. What were your feelings about his mediation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Ambassador Hill was not ambassador in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. He was ambassador to Macedonia. He had attended talks before. He wasn't seated at the table specifically, but he was there for the Pristina talks when we held talks in the writers' association in Kosovo and Metohija, the meeting that I referred to a while ago. I didn't deem it necessary to refer to Ambassador Hill specifically. I didn't understand why Ambassador Hill of all people should be the one to mediate these talks between Mr. Agani, as a representative of Kosovo and Metohija's Albanians on the one hand, and me as a representative of the Government of the Republic of Serbia on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, some moments ago we discussed the meeting that occurred on the 22nd of May, the meeting with Fehmi Agani, Blerim Shala, Veton Surroi, Mahmut Bakalli, Mr. Kelmendi, a meeting that took place in the headquarters of the writers' association of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you who attended the meeting. It's probably only now that you remember Ambassador Hill being there, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he wasn't with us at the table. He wasn't a participant in these talks. He was in the same meeting, but not at the same table.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this a bit further so it doesn't appear that I'm putting leading questions. Would you please explain the role of Ambassador Hill in that meeting held on the 22nd of May, if you know.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you, and I'm certain that my recollections are quite accurate. I went with an entire delegation, the second composition of the delegation. And in the hallway Mr. Veton Surroi addressed me and asked me whether I would agree to talk to Mr. Hill in one of the rooms of the writers' club. I refused that and I said that we came to talk with the delegation of Kosovo Albanians, not with Mr. Hill. That was the entire substance of that meeting. So I did not see Mr. Hill on that occasion, but I suppose that he was there, given that Mr. Surroi was offering me to meet with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us what was discussed on the 22nd of May with the Albanian representatives in that meeting, the one that you referred to just now.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The talks were not particularly meaningful. There were some general platitudes about how a political dialogue was needed, how it was important to resolve daily problems that civilians encountered. So this was more of an overture to future talks rather than talks on specific, concrete matters. There was really nothing to remember from that meeting. There was nothing of substance that took place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, on that occasion on the 22nd of May, was there any discussion of a new meeting of another date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. We did not schedule a particular date, but in principle we both expressed readiness to discuss these issues even though the logistics and modes of these future talks were not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, on the basis of those talks, did the delegation of the Government of Serbia go to Pristina again for talks on the 5th of June?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The delegation of the Government of Serbia, once again travelled to these talks for the same reasons, counting that there was some progress and that the talks would finally be launched. However, that was not the case. The talks did not take off except for the talks with other ethnic minorities in Kosovo, and the representatives of those two minor Albanian political parties. Only they were the ones who came; the others did not. It was my understanding that the Albanians - and when I say "Albanians," I'm referring to leaders of majority political parties - conceived these talks as exclusively talks between Serbs and Albanians as though there were only Serbs and Albanians living in Kosovo and no other ethnic communities, such as Turks, Gorani, Egyptians, and so on. It was our platform that we should take as a starting point the equal status of all ethnic communities and not accept that position, that there were no other ethnic communities in Kosovo but Albanian and Serbian ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, now let us go back to your correspondence with Professor Agani. He wrote a letter to you, you replied to him, and then on the 18th of June you travelled to Pristina. Did Professor Agani appear then?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not, and I waited for him for an exceptionally long time, for several hours, following which I returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, do you remember the resolution of the Security Council dated the 23rd of September, 1998, number 1199?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one thing, Mr. Zecevic. Did you mean the 18th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, it was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's in 93, line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps you should ask the witness again then, since you may have been thinking --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I misspoke when I asked you about the meeting with Professor Agani. I referred to the 18th of June, but since you exchanged those letters on the 17th of August, as you have already testified, you scheduled a meeting with him for the 18th of August, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I travelled on the 18th of August. I realised that you made a mistake, but I also realised that that was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, my question centred on the UN Resolution 1199, which is tab 18 here, P0456. Are you familiar with the content of this resolution, are you not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I am. I was still an unsuccessful head of the delegation for negotiations with Kosovo Albanians at the time, so naturally I followed all of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please look at page 2 of the resolution, last paragraph, where the Security Council calls upon the authorities and the Kosovo Albanian leadership to enter into dialogue. The delegation that you headed and the government, were they ready to enter the dialogue with the Kosovo Albanians as the Security Council Resolution requested you to do?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The government was ready and it based its position on the part of the resolution which says that the Security Council once again confirms the commitment of all member states to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That means that it was precisely that position of the Security Council that we used as a basis for insisting on these talks. In this resolution, the Security Council once again calls upon the authorities of FRY and the Kosovo Albanian leadership to enter immediately into meaningful dialogue without preconditions and with international involvement, and to a clear timetable leading to an end of the crisis and to negotiate a political solution to the issue of Kosovo. Therefore, in this resolution they guarantee the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which was a very strong encouragement for the Government of Serbia to persevere in their insistence to hold negotiations with the Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the text of this resolution, item 3 on the second page, the last paragraph, was quite acceptable to the Government of the Republic of Serbia and the delegation led by you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I see that you highlighted or emphasised the part of the resolution that speaks of the commitment of all member states to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That's on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain why you emphasised this, why you referred to this.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did that because as early as its first statement, its first announcement on the 10th of March, 1998, the government as well as the president of the Republic of Serbia in his declaration on the 18th of March, 1998, they both showed willingness to solve the issue of Kosovo and Metohija within the framework of the Republic of Serbia in compliance with the principle of territorial integrity and sovereignty of the Republic of Serbia. So in all of those appeals, that was the interpretation of the political dialogue. That is to say we were not considering the change of status of Kosovo and Metohija. And it was not supposed to become an independent state, rather the talks were aimed at establishing what scope of autonomy Kosovo wanted; that needed to be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Based on your experience and based on those infrequent contacts that you had with the representatives of Kosovo Albanians, tell us what was their position on that issue?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to distinguish between the Kosovo Albanians who came to talk with our delegation who had the same aims, who had the same intentions, as representatives of all other ethnic communities. So in the talks that we had with them they expressed the same efforts, the same convictions. And I suppose that the leaders of the majority political parties of Kosovo Albanians wanted something quite different. Later on we -- it became evident in Rambouillet. They did not want to sign the ten basic principles of the Contact Groups, precisely because one of those principles insisted on territorial integrity and sovereignty of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, in September the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia adopted a decision on the temporary Executive Council of the province of Kosovo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's tab 19, P907. Would you please explain this to us, since this was proposed by the government, and you were the deputy prime minister of the government.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, this decision of the government was an expression of the willingness to organise a cabinet in order to solve the daily -- the problems relating to the daily life in Kosovo and Metohija. So this temporary Executive Council of the province of Kosovo and Metohija was precisely a reflection of such intentions on the part of the Republic of Serbia; namely, efforts aimed at solving daily problems encountered by the population of Kosovo and Metohija regardless of their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, that was the reason why the government proposed to the National Assembly to pass a decision forming the provisional Executive Council of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, in 1998 did you meet with Ambassador Hill?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I met with Mr. Hill as well as Mr. O'Brien, who was a legal expert. Mr. Hill was not a lawyer. I met with them concerning the drafting of an agreement or perhaps a plan, perhaps I should call it a plan for self rule, in Kosovo and Metohija. Mr. Vladan Kutlesic was always a participant in such talks on our side. At the time he was deputy prime minister of the federal government. Both of us are constitutional lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain the process to us. This was the draft proposal or plan for self rule in Kosovo. Would you tell us how this transpired, how frequent these meetings were, over what period of time, and so on.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these meetings took place all the way up until 1999, if I remember well. The composition of delegations was always the same. In those meetings, Mr. Hill and Mr. O'Brien, or rather, to those meetings Mr. Hill and Mr. O'Brien would bring in their proposals for this plan or agreement on self-administration of Kosovo, we would give our comments, and then they would go with our comments to Kosovo and Metohija and then come back to us to convey to us whether the Kosovo Albanians accepted or not the suggestions given by us. There were -- I can't tell you how many versions of this plan for self-administration in Kosovo and Metohija. There were a lot of them. I know that I wrote an article for Politika concerning one of the last versions of this agreement, and as I was able to establish later, many of those ideas or solutions were later integrated into the draft agreement in Rambouillet, especially annex 1 or chapter 1 which was entitled "Constitution for Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, was President Milutinovic involved in the talks with Chris Hill?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, President Milutinovic was involved in those talks as well, quite actively so. However, the wording of the provisions was something that Mr. Kutlesic and I mostly dealt with it on our side, and it was Mr. O'Brien who did that on the US side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This contact with Mr. Hill and Mr. O'Brien and the exchange of drafts which, as you say, were taken to Kosovo in order to be discussed with the representatives of the majority political parties of Albanians, was that the kind of mediation that we discussed a bit earlier? Is that what you saw under this mediation role?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I understood under their mediation role. This is what the mediation boiled down to, namely, that the draft plan which was most likely produced by Mr. O'Brien would be given to us to comment upon them, and then they would take our comments to Pristina, obtain the opinion of Kosovo Albanians concerning them, and then convey that to us. So they were facilitators, they were mediators in these non-existing contacts between Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Kutlesic, and myself on one side and Kosovo Albanians on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you did not have any contact with the representatives of the majority Albanian parties in Kosovo, as I understood, because of their refusal to show up for talks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the date you mentioned, the 22nd of May, 1998, I think we never had any other contact with them. This includes the meetings in Rambouillet and Paris. In Rambouillet there was one instance of physical contact, but it was not a dialogue. It was a monologue by each side in the presence of Madeleine Albright.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, regardless of the mediating mission of Mr. Hill and Mr. O'Brien, as the delegation of the Serbian Assembly, you continued making attempts to invite the representatives of the majority Albanian parties for talks, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, because throughout this time we felt that direct contacts and direct talks were the most fruitful way to find a solution rather than talking through mediators who, let it be said, knew very little about the history of the problem, all the manifestations of the problem in the present, and who were not familiar with the spirit of our legal system either because these were people coming from a completely different legal system. The legal terminology was quite different. These were the reasons for the misunderstandings we had in our contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, do you remember that you sent a letter to Mr. Agani in early October 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at tab 22, 1D063. Is that your letter?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please briefly comment on this letter because -- well, especially on the last paragraph of this letter.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the letter for the umpteenth time, the conviction is expressed of the advantages of dialogue and solving all outstanding issues by political means in the interest of all the citizens and national or ethnic communities living in Kosovo and Metohija, and in the passage before the last it says that I'm asking Mr. Agani to consider this an open invitation, and I say that I hope we will soon have an opportunity to agree on a time for the continuation of the talks. In other words, to determine the date ourselves. However, this also remains simply a voice calling in the desert, crying out in the desert, without any response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you asked Professor Agani to consider this an open invitation, an open-ended call, does that mean that you were willing to meet him and talk to him at any time, anywhere?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the second sentence states that and clarifies it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, you remember a conversation -- well, you were aware that President Milosevic had talks with Mr. Holbrooke in early October 1998, and these led to an agreement. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement was presented to the cabinet. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The president of the republic, Milan Milutinovic, informed the cabinet of the content of those talks and that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And did the cabinet accept the agreement achieved between President Milosevic and Richard Holbrooke?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did and it established 11 points for the solution of the unresolved issue of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, are you aware that this fact was something that Yugoslavia informed the Security Council about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at tab 27, 1D204. Our then charge d'affaire in the mission to the United Nations in New York, Mr. Vladislav Jovanovic, signed the letter; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This letter contains the 11 points you mentioned which the Government of the Republic of Serbia adopted, does it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are set out in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it also contains a certain timetable or schedule containing the dates by which certain agreements were to be achieved and some sort of preparatory documents prepared, does it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dates are mentioned. You see, it's all in English. There's no need for me to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, that schedule mentioned here, of which the Security Council was notified, was also adopted by the government, was it not, on the same date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, tell me, to the best of your knowledge did the government implement this agreement, or rather, these 11 points which it adopted in October 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "implement." What do you imply by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, carry out.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, even after all of this you continued going to Kosovo, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in Kosovo with President Milutinovic on the 5th of November, 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. That was the second time President Milutinovic was going to Kosovo and Metohija with the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at tab 31, 1D40 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1D045.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the communique and the statement made for the public by President Milutinovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is it the one you have before you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, as we see, President Milutinovic is still referring to a firm agreement for the solution of all issues by political means.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He expressed the standpoint in the declaration of the 18th of March of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've said this, Professor, do you know whether President Milutinovic ever changed this standpoint?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 2 President Milutinovic in the passage before the last of his statement explains how the authorities and all of the Republic of Serbia sees the OSCE mission. Can you comment on this and was this the way you saw it also and was this is the position of the government, the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the reason why the OSCE mission was accepted, in the interest of finding out the truth about the events in Kosovo and Metohija and to deal with and get rid of media harangues, as is stated here, to present the truth to the world, eliminate rumours, speculation, and organise media incitement and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You said at the very outset that this was the second time that President Milutinovic went to Kosovo together with a delegation. Do you remember how many times in total President Milutinovic went to Kosovo with a delegation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember on one more occasion and that had to do with the signing of the so-called Pristina declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, tell me, what in your view was the reason why President Milutinovic went to Kosovo with the delegation for the meetings with the representatives of the majority Albanian parties?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was the one I've already mentioned. The high state official, the head of state, directly elected by the citizens, even though he had no strong effective constitutional power, wished by his presence to indicate the significance attached by the state to those talks to encourage and motivate the representatives of the majority Albanian parties for political dialogue and by presenting his ideas on what starting principles to adopt for the talks to contribute to the beginning of a dialogue. And these efforts are all evident in the president's declaration, his statement which sets out all these ideas, saying that closing themselves into a cultural and ethnic ghetto was not a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the third occasion on which President Milutinovic went to Kosovo. Please take a look at tab 33, 1D622, and this is his introductory statement at the talks with the representatives of national communities in Kosovo and Metohija, Pristina, 18th of November, 1998. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the president's keynote speech?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In his keynote speech the president again expressed his basic ideas, which were, so to speak, the red thread, a constant in his views on the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, this boiled down to the need for a political solution which was indispensable?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. That was the starting point in President Milutinovic's ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at 1D623, these are the concluding remarks by the president. Do you remember his concluding remarks at that same meeting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, do you remember that President Milutinovic too sent letters to the Albanian leaders, in a bid to in a way encourage them, stimulate them, to attend meetings with the delegation, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who he sent those letters to, the political leaders or also prominent members of the Albanian community in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He sent letters to both, he sent letters to the political leaders, the political leaders of the Albanian ethnic community, Mr. Qausha, Hyseni, Demaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, both the government and the president did their best. How can we understand this? An attempt was made to talk to the Albanian leaders at all costs, or perhaps there's a different interpretation that you would suggest?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an effort that was made to encourage those most prominent among Kosovo's Albanians. For example, Mr. Qausha has an academic reputation, not merely a political one. An attempt, as I said, to talk, to use their authority, to use their reputation in order to contribute to political talks and in order to stop armed clashes throughout Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at tab 36, Professor, 1D066, are these the letters that we have been mentioning, the letters to Qausha, to Demaqi, to Hyseni?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are the very letters. Their substance is identical. They were just sent to different persons, and I explained why these very persons. These are important persons in the Albanian ethnic community. These are not just politicians. Their importance is not solely political.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think it's time, Your Honours, for a break. I definitely need one I can tell you -- I can assure you that and Professor too, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Professor, that's it for today. The usher will escort you from the court, and we'll continue tomorrow at 9.00. [The witness stands down].
